newsitem.title: USA: Make personal security a safe investment.
newsitem.headline: Make personal security a safe investment.

text.p: (Part 1 of a two-part series on personal and home security. Next week's column will deal with home security.)
By Judith Schoolman
The word bodyguard often conjures up images of great hulking monsters with dark sunglasses who look as if they could crush a man with their bare hands.
When people think "bodyguard" they often think "thug," exactly NOT the kind of person to hire when seeking personal protection.

Rather than smash heads, trained bodyguards -- now formally known as personal protection agents -- should use them. Their mission is to keep their charges from harm by advance planning, organisation and preparation. The key is avoiding dangerous situations, not figuring out what to do once you're in one.

Bodyguards are not only for heads of state or celebrities and they should not be confused with security guards, such as those who patrol shopping malls or office buildings. They provide specific protection to an individual who fears for his or her personal safety, or the safety of family, friends or guests.

The safest individuals, regardless of wealth or notoriety, are those who do not call attention to themselves. Security experts say that living as low-key as possible is often the best protection for someone who feels his social prominence, wealth or position could make him a target of crime or assault.

"Put yourself in the place of a corporate executive. A thug as a bodyguard would definately stand out," said Jim King, executive director of the International Association of Personal Protection Agents.

"A personal protection agent has to blend in, not look like a former NFL player or a professional wrestler," King said. "They have to be well groomed, mature and able to carry on a conversation," he added, not be some 21-year-old who's more interested in dancing with the girls than keeping his charge from potential harm.
Given threats of kidnapping, assault or robbery, some individuals seek personal protection for specific events such as a party or for limited periods of time such as vacations.
Hiring personal protection takes more than looking for a former member of the military, a retired policeman or someone who advertises in paramilitary magazines.

"Being an ex-cop or an ex-military has nothing to do with personal protection," King said from the association's headquarters in Brighton, Tenn. "The skills are not necessarily transferrable," although the discipline and weapons training are added assets.
"Having these attributes is great, but don't hire solely on this."

Carrying a gun is also not a prerequisite. "Ninty-nine percent of the time you don't need guns. The Secret Service don't often shoot, neither do professional government agents," he said. State weapons laws vary and could provide problems for the agent if travelling across state lines.
What is most important is proper training, experience and maturity, King said.

Don't hire a bodyguard through the Yellow Pages. Many, if not all, of the security companies that advertise provide security workers for malls and commercial buildings. Often, King said, these people receive little or no training. One could be a mall security agent one day, and the next day be told to come in wearing a suit to be a bodyguard, he said.
As in most cases involving personal care, referrals from trusted individuals are the easiest and best route to take.

The International Association of Personal Protection Agents, a professional organisation, provides referrals for its approximately 400 individual and agency members located in most states and 24 foreign countries. The member agencies do background checks of their employees, who also must pass psychological tests, King said.
Experts also advise against using classified ads in magazines for hiring or seeking personal protection agents.

While legitimate bodyguard companies do not advertise, their services do become well known. In Hollywood, for example, the Gavin Debecker agency is known to provide quality bodyguards for celebrities.

The services of a professional bodyguard cost about $250 a day plus expenses, such as travel, food, lodging, appropriate clothes and all other extras. Most states have their own licensing authority for the various services a bodyguard might provide, such as a security license or a private investigator's license. Currently, Virginia and Texas require a license for bodyguards.
Legitimate agencies will also draft contracts for the service. If the person or group you are dealing with does not provide a written contract, look elsewhere.
For additional information on hiring personal protection agents, contact the International Association of Personal Protection Agents, 901-837-1915.

Regarding the recent column on tips when booking hotel rooms, a writer said that one of the latest penalties hotels are imposing on guests is for early checkout. In some hotels, guests who stay more than one night are asked to initial their departure date and if they leave early they are charged. Guests should inquire about this policy, the writer advises.
